Congruences via Partitions with Exactly Two Part Sizes

Sittinon Jirattikansakul Address: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok 10330, Thailand, and Centre of Excellence in Mathematics, Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, Thailand Email address: sittinon.j@chula.ac.th , Teeradej Kittipassorn Address: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok 10330, Thailand, and Centre of Excellence in Mathematics, Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, Thailand Email address: teeradej.k@chula.ac.th , Kraiwich Kongsiri Address: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok 10330, Thailand Email address: 6634303123@student.chula.ac.th , Nitipon Moonwichit Address: Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Claremont Graduate University, Claremont, CA, USA Email address: nitipon.moonwichit@cgu.edu and Kirati Sriamorn Address: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok 10330, Thailand Email address: kirati.s@chula.ac.th
Abstract.

We prove the congruence ∑1≤k<Nσ0​(N−k2)≡0(mod4)\sum_{1\leq k<\sqrt{N}}\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2})\equiv 0\pmod{4}, where σ0​(m)\sigma_{0}(m) denotes the number of positive divisors of mm, for N=A​n+BN=An+B with (A,B)∈{(16,14),(A,B)\in\{(16,14), (36,30),(36,30), (72,42),(72,42), (196,70),(196,70), (252,114)}(252,114)\}. Our proof relies on a result of Keith which states that ν2​(N)≡0(mod4)\nu_{2}(N)\equiv 0\pmod{4}, where ν2​(N)\nu_{2}(N) is the number of partitions of NN with exactly two part sizes. Inspired by Dewitt and Keith, our approach combines combinatorial arguments with modular arithmetic techniques.

1. Introduction

Integer partitions play a central role in number theory and combinatorics. Since the foundational work of Euler [4], partitions have been studied from a variety of perspectives, including generating functions by Andrews [2], asymptotic analysis by Hardy and Ramanujan [5], and geometric interpretations via Ferrers and Young diagrams by MacMahon [8], among many others.

Define νk​(N)\nu_{k}(N) to be the number of partitions of NN in which exactly kk sizes of part appear. For example, ν2​(4)=2\nu_{2}(4)=2 since all partitions of 4 with exactly two part sizes are (3,1)(3,1) and (2,1,1)(2,1,1), and ν3​(4)=0\nu_{3}(4)=0 since no partition of 4 has exactly three part sizes.

This counting function has been studied by MacMahon [9], Andrews [1], and Tani and Bouroubi [10] where the first two independently derived a compact formula for the case k=2k=2 as

ν2​(N)=12​(∑k=1N−1σ0​(k)​σ0​(N−k)−σ1​(N)+σ0​(N))\displaystyle\nu_{2}(N)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\sigma_{0}(k)\sigma_{0}(N-k)-\sigma_{1}(N)+\sigma_{0}(N)\right)

where σ0​(N)\sigma_{0}(N) is the number of positive divisors of NN and σ1​(N)\sigma_{1}(N) is the sum of the positive divisors of NN. Keith [7] then later proved that ν2​(A​n+B)≡0(mod4)\nu_{2}(An+B)\equiv 0\pmod{4} when (A,B)(A,B) is one of (16,14), (36,30), (72,42), (196,70) and (252,114). This inspires us to revisit several results of Keith [3] using a finer combinatorial approach based on multiset partition. In particular, we study configurations of Young diagrams of partitions of NN with exactly two part sizes in the arithmetic sequences considered by Keith [7], and obtain the following congruence.

Theorem 1.

Let (A,B)∈{(16,14),(36,30),(72,42),(196,70),(252,114)}(A,B)\in\{(16,14),(36,30),(72,42),(196,70),(252,114)\} and N=A​n+BN=An+B for some nonnegative integer nn. Then

∑1≤k<Nσ0​(N−k2)≡0(mod4).\sum\limits_{1\leq k<\sqrt{N}}\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2})\equiv 0\pmod{4}.

The sum ∑1≤k<Nσ0​(N−k2)\sum_{1\leq k<\sqrt{N}}\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2}) in Theorem 1 and its asymptotic behavior were investigated by Hooley [6] in his study of representations of NN as the sum of a square and a product where the number of such representations is equal to ∑−N<k<Nσ0​(N−k2)\sum_{-\sqrt{N}<k<\sqrt{N}}\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2}).

The following corollaries are consequences of Theorem 1.

Corollary 2.

Let NN be a positive integer such that N≡14(mod16)N\equiv 14\pmod{16} or N≡70(mod196)N\equiv 70\pmod{196}. Then the number of positive odd integers kk such that k2<Nk^{2}<N and σ0​(N−k2)≡2(mod4)\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2})\equiv 2\pmod{4} is always even.

Corollary 3.

Let NN be a positive integer such that N≡B(modA)N\equiv B\pmod{A} where (A,B)(A,B) is one of (36,30),(72,42),(36,30),(72,42), and (252,114)(252,114). Then

∑1≤k<N3∤kσ0​(N−k2)≡0(mod4).\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k<\sqrt{N}\\ 3\nmid k\end{subarray}}\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2})\equiv 0\pmod{4}.

To prove Theorem 1, we first prove an auxiliary congruence relation in Theorem 4 by assuming a weaker assumption on the natural number NN.

Theorem 4.

Let NN be a natural number satisfying

  • •

    NN cannot be written as a sum of two squares, and

  • •

    N=2​mN=2m for some odd integer mm.

Then

ν2​(N)+∑1≤k<Nσ0​(N−k2)+12​σ1​(N)≡0(mod4).\nu_{2}(N)+\sum\limits_{1\leq k<\sqrt{N}}\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2})+\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{1}(N)\equiv 0\pmod{4}.

Note that according to the formula for ν2​(N)\nu_{2}(N) given in the introduction, the congruence in Theorem 4 can be written as

12​(σ0​(N)+∑k=1N−1σ0​(k)​σ0​(N−k))+∑1≤k<Nσ0​(N−k2)≡0(mod4).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\sigma_{0}(N)+\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\sigma_{0}(k)\sigma_{0}(N-k)\right)+\sum_{1\leq k<\sqrt{N}}\sigma_{0}(N-k^{2})\equiv 0\pmod{4}.

To the best of our knowledge, this congruence does not appear explicitly in the existing literature.

We organize the rest of the paper as follows. In Section 2, we discuss background and terminology. Section 3 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1, which serves as our main result. In Section 4, we apply Theorem 1 and use some elementary number theory to prove Corollaries 2 and 3. Finally, in Section 5, we conclude the paper with some remarks and a conjecture inspired by our findings.

2. Background

Fix a natural number nn. A partition of nn with exactly one part size is a tuple v→=(n1,n1,…,n1)\vec{v}=(n_{1},n_{1},\ldots,n_{1}) of kk copies of n1n_{1} for some k≥1k\geq 1 satisfying k​n1=nkn_{1}=n. A partition of nn with exactly two part sizes is a tuple v→=(n1,n1,…,n1,n2,n2,…,n2)\vec{v}=(n_{1},n_{1},\ldots,n_{1},n_{2},n_{2},\ldots,n_{2}) where n1>n2≥1n_{1}>n_{2}\geq 1 such that if n1n_{1} appears k1k_{1} times and n2n_{2} appears k2k_{2} times, then k1​n1+k2​n2=nk_{1}n_{1}+k_{2}n_{2}=n. In this paper, when we mention a rectangle, we mean a usual rectangular grid where each cell is a square. An m×nm\times n rectangle is a rectangle consisting of mm rows and nn columns. If XX is an m×nm\times n rectangle, denote by XTX^{T} the n×mn\times m rectangle.

A Young diagram for a partition is the unique grid of cells where the cells are arranged in left-justified rows with the row lengths in non-increasing order. For each Young diagram consisting of nn cells in kk rows, we associate the diagram with the tuple (n1,n2,…,nk)(n_{1},n_{2},\ldots,n_{k}) where nin_{i} is the number of cells lying in the ii-th row. By this interpretation, each Young diagram in rectangular shape consisting of nn cells uniquely determines the partition of nn with exactly one part size. Likewise, each Young diagram in L-shape uniquely determines the partition of nn with exactly two part sizes. For example, Figure 1(a) is interpreted as the partition (3,3,3,3)(3,3,3,3) of 1212, and Figure 1(b) is interpreted as the partition (5,5,5,2,2)(5,5,5,2,2) of 1919.

Any Young diagram corresponding to a partition with exactly two part sizes can be viewed as obtained by gluing two rectangles vertically, with the rectangle having the wider base placed on top. Conversely, every such L-shaped diagram can be decomposed in this way into a unique pair of rectangles. This observation motivates our approach and leads to a proof based on counting pairs of rectangles.

3. Proof of Theorem 1

Let NN be a natural number that cannot be written as a sum of two squares. A canonical pair for NN is an unordered pair of rectangles {X,Y}\{X,Y\} such that the numbers of rows of XX and YY are fewer than or equal to the numbers of columns of XX and YY, respectively, and the sum of numbers of cells of XX and YY is NN. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the multiset consisting of

{X,Y},{X,YT},{XT,Y},{XT,YT}\{X,Y\},\{X,Y^{T}\},\{X^{T},Y\},\{X^{T},Y^{T}\}

for all canonical pairs {X,Y}\{X,Y\} for NN. We define subsets ℬ,𝒞,𝒟\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}, and ℰ\mathcal{E} of 𝒜\mathcal{A} as follows:

ℬ\displaystyle\mathcal{B} ={{X,Y}∈𝒜|the numbers of columns of X and Y are different},\displaystyle=\{\{X,Y\}\in\mathcal{A}\ |\ \text{the numbers of columns of $X$ and $Y$ are different}\},
𝒞\displaystyle\mathcal{C} ={{X,Y}∈𝒜|X or Y is a square},\displaystyle=\{\{X,Y\}\in\mathcal{A}\ |\ \text{$X$ or $Y$ is a square}\},
𝒟\displaystyle\mathcal{D} ={{X,Y}∈𝒜|the numbers of columns of X and Y are the same},\displaystyle=\{\{X,Y\}\in\mathcal{A}\ |\ \text{the numbers of columns of $X$ and $Y$ are the same}\},
ℰ\displaystyle\mathcal{E} ={{X,Y}∈𝒜|X=YT}.\displaystyle=\{\{X,Y\}\in\mathcal{A}\ |\ \text{$X=Y^{T}$}\}.

From the definitions above, there is a natural correspondence among the partitions with at most two part sizes, rectangular and L-shaped Young diagrams, and pairs of rectangles. As noted at the end of Section 2, {X,Y}\{X,Y\} corresponds to the Young diagram obtained by placing the rectangle with the wider base on top; in case where the bases are equal, either rectangle can be placed on top (resulting in the same diagram). This means 𝒜\mathcal{A} can be viewed as the multiset of Young diagrams obtained from all possible vertical gluings of two rectangles, where each rectangle may independently be replaced by its transpose. Consequently, the purpose of defining ℬ,𝒞,𝒟\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}, and ℰ\mathcal{E} is to classify those diagrams and count their multiplicities. We may interpret the sets as follows:

  • •

    ℬ\mathcal{B} is the set of all Young diagrams corresponding to the partitions of NN with exactly two part sizes,

  • •

    𝒞\mathcal{C} is the set of all Young diagrams corresponding to the partitions of NN that can be decomposed into a pair of rectangles {X,Y}\{X,Y\} such that at least one of them is a square,

  • •

    𝒟\mathcal{D} is the multiset of Young diagrams with exactly one part size where we will later show how to count the multiplicities in Lemma .

  • •

    ℰ\mathcal{E} is the set of all Young diagrams corresponding to the partitions of NN that can be decomposed into a pair of rectangles {X,Y}\{X,Y\} such that X=YTX=Y^{T}.

Denote by ⋆\star the gluing operation and define X⋆YX\star Y to be the multiset consisting of

{X,Y},{X,YT},{XT,Y},{XT,YT}\{X,Y\},\{X,Y^{T}\},\{X^{T},Y\},\{X^{T},Y^{T}\}

for any {X,Y}∈𝒜\{X,Y\}\in\mathcal{A}. Here, {X,Y},{X,YT},{XT,Y},{XT,YT}\{X,Y\},\{X,Y^{T}\},\{X^{T},Y\},\{X^{T},Y^{T}\} can be viewed as the Young diagrams we mentioned above. See Figure 3 for an example. The figure demonstrates the four canonical pairs for 66 together with their associated gluings. There are nine diagrams (with repetitions) in 𝒜\mathcal{A} corresponding to six elements in ℬ\mathcal{B}. Since ℬ\mathcal{B} is a set, and among these nine diagrams there are three pairs of identical diagrams, each of these pairs is counted only once in ℬ\mathcal{B}. A similar argument applies to 𝒞,𝒟\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}, and ℰ\mathcal{E}. Therefore, at N=6N=6,

|𝒜|=16=6+4+5+1=|ℬ|+|𝒞|+|𝒟|+|ℰ|.|\mathcal{A}|=16=6+4+5+1=|\mathcal{B}|+|\mathcal{C}|+|\mathcal{D}|+|\mathcal{E}|.
